transcription.text: Welcome, John Spiro. Welcome, everybody. We might start with our second session. And this
panel session is looking at the role of repair in product stewardship and the circular economy.
And I'll hand it over to John Gutsakis from eWasteWatch, who's going to chair this. But
I'd like to welcome Spiro Kalos from the Australian Mobile Telecommunications Association and Mobile
Muster, Janet Leslie, who's on my left, Australian Information Industry Association and Ian McAllister
from the Consumer Electronic Suppliers Association. So over to you, John. Thank you very much.
Thank you. Thank you very much, Leanne. And well done to you and Griffith and all of the
participants in running this event today. It's a great opportunity to kick off a broader
discussion around the role of repair and durability and where it relates to the Australian context
is really, really important. So big thanks to everyone for being part of this. We've
got three key associations here with us and very grateful to the AAIA, to CESA and AMTA
for joining us. It really is important that we have industry participating in these sorts
of discussions. And so thanks again to Janet, Spiro and to Ian. As many of you will know,
prolonging the life value and functionality of products and components and materials is
a key circular economy principle. So what's the relevance of increased repairability for
industry product stewardship schemes where manufacturers and brands are taking greater
responsibility for their products cradle to cradle? To what extent is repairability an
important element of product stewardship schemes moving forward? And what are some
of the barriers and what are some of the opportunities? Our panellists will share their views and
insights on some of these questions in the time that we have. But if we're serious about
waste avoidance and waste reduction in Australia and the practical implementation of circular
economy principles, we do need to move up the waste management hierarchy faster and
we need to do it with genuine conviction. And that's very, very important. The time
is right to repair, but it does require policies and programs that acknowledge the barriers
and the opportunities to making it work as a waste avoidance and reduction strategy.
And we mustn't overlook the social and the cultural dimension when we're talking about
repair. Repair is just as much about empowering consumers to take control of the products
they purchase and own. And it is as it is about waste reduction. And we've heard various
commentary and discussion from other panellists and speakers today about the role of the consumer
and what the market is saying in parts that they want. In Australia, we have the National
Waste Policy Action Plan. If that plan is serious about waste avoidance and reduction,
then product durability, repairability, reusability and improved recycling and recyclability
is really, really important, especially as it relates to meeting growing consumer expectations
about the goods that we use every day in all spheres of life. So let me introduce our panellists
in a little bit more detail. It's important as part of setting that context. Janet Leslie
is the Chair of the CSR Policy Advisory Network with the Australian Information Industry Association.
Janet's also the Sustainability Manager for Canon Oceania. Canon, of many of the brands
that I've come across over the years in Australia, has a long history of taking a full life cycle
approach to product design. And Janet's been very active for over a decade in various programs,
Cartridges for Planet Arc, the NTCRS, the Australian Battery Recycling Initiative, and is here today
as Chair of the Australian Information Industry CSR's Policy Advisory Network. Janet's also
a Director of the Australia and New Zealand Recycling Platform and one of the leading
not-for-profit industry-run co-regulatory arrangements under the National Television
and Computer Recycling Scheme, a strong advocate for national multi-stakeholder product stewardship
schemes. I'll quickly introduce Spiro and Ian as well, so we can get those done and
you can know who's talking to you today. But Spiro Kalos is the Head of Product Stewardship
for the Australian Mobile Telecommunications Association, and he also manages the Mobile
Master Programme. Over two decades of experience with the telco industry, Spiro is one of Australia's
experts in e-waste and mobile phone recycling. As the Head of Product Stewardship for Amta,
Spiro manages the government-accredited stewardship programme, Mobile Master, which is funded
voluntarily by the major handset manufacturers and the network providers, the telcos. Mobile
Master is very active, committed to raising awareness and educating the community on how
and why we should all be recycling more, along with tackling the barriers to reuse and repair.
Ian McAllister, the CEO of the Consumer Electronics Suppliers Association, and Ian has also been
very active in the industry, in the sector for many years. He is the CEO of CESA and
also the Director of Strathair Link Consulting. Ian's got over 30 years' experience in ICT
industry policy development, government relations, regulatory policy formulation in Australia
and in the APEC region, and like Janet, had deep involvement in the development of the
Product Stewardship Act, the NTCRS, and the continuing body of work that's been going
on in the electrical electronics equipment space in Australia. But now, if we could really
hand over, if I can hand over to Janet first to give us a snapshot, some insights of what's
happening in her industry and around IT and how it relates to repair in product stewardship.
Over to you, Janet.
Okay, thanks, John. So, as John said, I'm here, I'm from Canon, but I'm the Chair of our
AAA CSR Policy Advisory Network, and that's most of the major hardware and software brands
in the IT sector, so Canon, Dell, HP, IBM, brother Cisco, Microsoft. So, I really related
to what Stuart said about giving 10 years of his life to get the motor vehicle scheme
up and running. Both Ian and I, and John, gave at least 10 years to getting the national
TV and computer and recycling scheme up and running, and as John said, it's still an ongoing
piece of work there. So, although we're fierce competitors when it comes to selling our products,
on a lot of environmental issues, we think it makes sense to collaborate, and it's better
for our customers and better for us, and for the community as well. So, that's why we do
have all these product stewardship schemes that we support. For those who don't know
about the national TV and computer recycling scheme, all of the people who import TVs and
computers into Australia, including printers, are required to collect and recycle those
products according to national standards, protecting health and safety environmental
standards, and generally speaking, that scheme's been pretty successful. So, I thought I'd just
mention, before I talk about the Productivity Commission report and the recommendations
about product stewardship, I thought I'd just mention some of the things that our OEMs have
in place already. So, in terms of product design, which is obviously where it all starts,
we all have and write quite a lot of information about our rigorous programs to design products
that are not only more useful for our customers, but also to reduce the environmental impact
at every stage of their life cycle. So, we're making smaller, lighter products with fewer
resources, more renewable resources, more durable, and just from our own industry, for example,
in printers, and we've heard some remarks about cartridges and what have you today,
but so in our industry now we're moving to mega tank printers, so they're printers with
large refillable ink tanks, long lasting, and we have long warranties on our cameras.
All of the OEMs have repair and reuse programs in place, so a lot of our products are actually
leased and then brought back to us, and most of us, some companies repair parts and products in
Australia, but a lot of us have international hubs where we send products for repair and reuse
and then for selling into different markets. So, there's a fair amount of repair and reuse going
on already through those sort of programs. Most of us sell second-hand products as well,
refurbished products, and in Canon's case, just addressing the point that Erin made about printers,
we've tried to address some of the issues that people have with printers by having a
hotline, 24-hour hotline, that will really help people get things to work properly.
So, I guess I just wanted to say that because there are a lot of initiatives that are already
happening and that people perhaps don't know about, but in terms of responding to the
Productivity Commission report, first of all, we welcome the finding that there's little evidence
of OEMs deliberately designing for obsolescence. That's certainly our experience. Our equipment's
becoming more and more reliable all the time. We also welcome the proposal for the ACCC to
provide advice on warranty periods. It's always a really tricky thing for us to sort of compare
our expectations and consumers' expectations with how long a product will last, how long you need
to keep parts, how to update software programs when operating systems are changing. So, I think
to have a general consensus on some of those things would be really helpful. In the National
TV and Computer Scheme, we're a bit uncertain about the proposal to include repair targets in
the NTCRS, and I think, well, we certainly want to be involved in the discussion because when we
designed that scheme, it was very much designed as an end-of-life scheme, and the idea was that
repair would be encouraged and that products would be funneled into the repair options before they
came back for end-of-life recycling. So, it was never designed to be anti-repair or anything like that,
and we're just not sure how you would change the scheme to include
repaired products within the targets. But we do have, and our past experience is that
the products that come back through the NTCRS are, generally speaking, really old
and not really fit for reuse. We're actually doing, one of our members is doing a survey on that
right at the moment. We think there's a need for further work to understand the repair industry
and the asset management industry in our sector. There's not a lot of data available
because the targets at the moment only relate to the regulated part of the industry, so there's a
whole market out there that's not regulated, that's not really covered. We did have one idea
about the targets, and that is that because it's a mature scheme now, we've got a target of
80% of whatever we sell essentially has to get recycled by a certain time, which is pretty much
an unachievable target. We think that probably, if you did away with that target altogether
and you had a measure that was actually, this scheme has to be readily available to anybody
who wants to dispose of an end-of-life device, that that would be one way then of,
we call it the convenience model. That would be one way then maybe you could just include
repair in there somehow as well. I guess the other point is about tracking devices.
At ANZRP, we already do include tracking devices in the e-waste, and we've actually
stopped using a couple of recyclers because our products have ended up in interesting places.
But one of the issues that would need to be dealt with is the legislation about,
what's it called? Tracking. You can't put a tracking device in something without
telling somebody. I've just forgotten the, yeah. Surveillance legislation, that's it, yeah.
So we can do it because we've got contracts with our recyclers and contracts with our
transport providers, and in those contracts we say we'll include tracking devices.
But that's probably enough from me, and I'll hand back to John, I guess.
Thanks, Janet. Thanks, Janet. Thanks for the overview, and for, I suppose, exposing
some information about programs and services initiatives that parts of the market,
some consumers might know about. So very useful information. If we can move on to you now, Ian,
from the Consumer Electronics Suppliers Association, to give us a snapshot of your
industry, your membership, and some insights and views, your position on the
Productivity Commission draft report as well. So over to you, Ian.
Thanks, John. I've just got to get a brief overview of what CESA's position is on this
issue and make some comments on some of the recommendations by the Productivity Commission.
As John mentioned earlier, CESA's the premier national industry body representing the consumer
electronics industry generally. Our members are well-placed to comment on possible policy options
to address perceived barriers to repair. As they are predominantly global suppliers,
so our membership are the Samsungs and LGs and Energizers and Mieles, Electroluxes of this world,
all the brands that you're familiar with. Our members are well-acquainted with the EU
Eco-Design Directive. In fact, Australia's rather following what's happening in many other
jurisdictions around the world. So we're very close, we work closely with our sister organisations in
Europe, APEA and AHEM in the United States, where they're currently involved in the 27 states that
have legislative proposals on these issues. So we're close to what's happening worldwide.
Our members have well-established repair facilities, both in-house and third-party
authorised repair networks. So over many decades they've undertaken the vast majority of consumer
electronics repair, particularly in the warranty space. CESA strongly believes the scope of future
RTR proposals, if justified, and demonstrating a net benefit to the community, so you have to get
over the hoops of regulatory impact statements and so on. Once they're justified, we believe
these proposals should be confined to major household appliances in the consumer electronics
sector and focus on professional repairers, such as in the Eco-Design Directive. The professional
repairer does not necessarily have to be one directly employed or contracted by the supplier.
To CESA, this could be an independent body, as long as the repairers are able to demonstrate
they comply with applicable regulations and standards, that they are covered by relevant
insurance, covering liabilities resulting from the offered service, particularly in the electrical
safety and cyber security space. In the Australian context, we believe it is important that such
services should be nationwide and take account of Australia's unique consumer laws,
electrical safety standards and regulatory arrangements under the Product Stewardship
Act or Product Stewardship Schemes. We strongly believe that a substantial data analysis mapping
of the repair sector is required in order to make evidence-based proposals for future policy
or regulatory options. We consider right to repair proposals should focus upon products
and repair markets where there is evidence of low durability of products, lack of repair facilities
and insufficient nationwide coverage. I'll just tackle a couple of the issues we put to the
commission in our submission, things we highlighted. We believe the Australian
consumer law provides very strong protection for consumers in Australia,
far greater than many other jurisdictions. Consumers have incredible protections under the ACL.
In addition, the durability of consumer electronics has vastly improved over time.
Only when the case for lack of repair and service data sharing has been clearly proven,
this is where I think a lot more analysis needs to be done. Once it's clearly proven,
only then should any mandatory obligations be considered. In the consumer electronics sector,
it has become increasingly difficult to identify and locate suitable,
qualified professional repairers, particularly in the rural and regional areas. This is due to lack
of training, ageing workforce. These are real issues for our companies because they can't
get enough people to do their own warranty of repairs, let alone post-warranty.
We believe available evidence does not point to a systematic competition problem. We believe in
the consumer electronics industry that Part 4 of the Act is suitable to address any competitive
repair activities. We don't think there's any necessity there for proposals. We do not consider
current intellectual property protections pose a barrier to consumer electronics repair in
Australia. That's our position. You may not agree with that, but that's our position and we'd like
to see evidence where it has done that. Just a couple of points on the findings of the Commission,
the report recommendations. CESA strongly endorses the Commission's recommendations
for further analysis to determine whether barriers to repair are generating harm in any
given sector and that in-depth case-by-case analysis in both the repair market and the
primary market for all products is required prior to implementing positive obligations.
It's very important for CESA members that the Commission distinguish between product markets.
The consumer electronics sector is very different to the agricultural machinery sector.
It's very different to the motor vehicle sector or therapeutic goods.
For example, we don't have tens of thousands of repairers out there such as the
AAA people have. We have different requirements for installations,
heating and cooling systems, air conditioning, gas, where the installers are involved. Very
different issues there. We agree with the Commission's findings that the repair activity
is diminishing in the electronic sector as replacement tends to be more attractive due
to rapidly falling prices, durability and consumer preferences for up-to-date services.
CESA does not support and has some reservations with the Commission's recommendations regarding
changes to the NTCRS scheme to facilitate repair and reuse. We believe there are adequate and
comprehensive policies and regulations already in place to address the e-waste issue and that
perhaps should be left to the Environment Department to work on. Our position is that
the NTCRS scheme, as Janet just said, is a scheme for recycling. It's of only a segment
of the e-waste area. It's only two lines, computers and televisions. There's a vast
amount of other e-waste generated out there that have not been included in the NTCRS scheme.
Despite industry, we have been lobbying for years and years for the Government to pick up
the WeDirective in Europe and add many other e-waste streams to the NTCRS scheme but it has
fallen on deaf ears to date. The NTCRS scheme was not designed for reuse and refurbishment.
It's an end-of-life issue, not a prolonged life scheme. We do question how co-regulatory bodies
suggested in the report could undertake repairs, who would fund the repairs, who would own the
repaired products and who would take responsibility for the repaired product, particularly in regard
to electrical safety and data security once it was repaired.
An issue brought up by the AAA people this morning was it's a good idea on the lobbying
side for people in the industry trying to build a repair industry not to muddy the waters by
focusing on more than one portfolio. I agree with their suggestion that they should stick to
Treasury and ACCC, those sorts of issues, rather than muddying the waters with Department of
Environment and Product Stewardship schemes. That's about all I have to say.
Thanks, Ian. Thank you kindly for that. Thanks for your frank and candid views and position on
these issues. Many of the issues you raise, the questions that you pose, are really being in part
addressed by the review of the Product Stewardship Act, where there are several recommendations
looking to deal with the role of repair, reuse, durability and recyclability in relation to
electrical and electronic products, and also the draft report from the Productivity Commission.
I think your point around the need to look more specifically at product class by product class
in many respects is really important. It's not a one size fits all when it comes down to very
specific and practical measures to look at the issue of repair and improving the rate of repair
where appropriate. So we do need to, in my view, look at product class by product class and what
does that mean and what are the opportunities. I think one of the challenges here for all of us is
how we do work together in a constructive way, how we do collaborate, how we do reflect the
wishes of the market, understand the constraints of the producers and all of the other stakeholders
that are involved. But I think in part it is about how we flip those things which we see
as roadblocks, as barriers to repair. Can these be transformed into opportunities, new industries,
where there are issues that are simply too problematic or there is no net benefit
environmentally, economically, socially, then we need to decide accordingly. So there is a need to,
in some respects, as I say, within a stewardship context, look at a very practical expression of
what a circular economy means for product stewardship programs. And that requires collaboration,
not combat. Our next speaker, Spiro Kalos. If I can pass on to you, Spiro, to
share your views and position and insights in relation to repair.
Yeah, thank you. Good afternoon all and thank you, John, and to the organisers of this event and for
the opportunity to be a part of today's discussions. So the Australian Mobile Telecommunications
Association, or better known as ANTA, is an industry association and our members include
the network providers, network infrastructure companies and also the handset manufacturers.
Now, my role within ANTA is to head up Mobile Master, which is an industry-led
product stewardship scheme voluntarily funded by its members, which again include handset
manufacturers. And what makes us quite unique is the network carriers. So Vodafone, Telstra and
Optus are all funding members of the program. We've been operating for over 23 years and
formerly accredited in 2014 under what was the Product Stewardship Act of 2011.
Now, in that time, we've collected and recycled over 1,600 tonnes of product,
including handsets, batteries and accessories, effectively diverting this product from ending
up in the general waste stream. The product scope for us has expanded since the program
established itself in 1998. And at that time, it was to tackle the issue that was
mobile phone batteries. From a repair perspective, we want and encourage people to think about
reusing or repairing their mobiles as it is an important step in extending the life cycle of
these devices. And as we know, repair is a complex issue and it does vary from product to product,
and especially when acknowledging that there are already established repair
frameworks for some of these product streams. So our research indicates that one in three
consumers have actually repaired a mobile phone and with 60% of those individuals utilising the
services of an independent repair store. But I only expect these numbers are actually going to
continue to grow. What I might just add here is earlier we heard from the Commissioner make the
comments that the electronics repair industry has been shrinking. In our space, it's a growth
channel for us in terms of volume of product being collected year on year. And we've seen growth
coming from the independent repair work, year on year growth over the last four years. And we also
have over 300 independent repair stores that are currently participating in the program.
There's a couple of areas within the draft report that I'd like to make some specific
comments on. The first one being around software updates for a reasonable period of time.
And something that is already happening within the mobile phone industry with most brands supporting
updates for a minimum of two years. But what we are seeing is that updates are being used as a
competitive advantage against the brands themselves. So just a couple of examples,
Nokia recently announced a campaign called Love It, Trust It, Keep It. And they're encouraging
their customers to hold on to their devices for longer and supporting them with software and
security updates of three years. Samsung only recently, in fact last week, announced security
updates of up to five years across their devices. But ultimately, the flow and effect here is that
consumers hold on to the devices for a longer period of time. And so the average ownership
now is sitting at over 2.7 years. Secondly, I just want to touch on the role of product stewardship.
And I guess that's where my experience lies. So historically, in this country, product stewardship
has been about collecting and recycling product. Now, I'm a supporter of mobile must becoming more
than that and actively encouraging consumers to play their part within the circular economy.
What we do know is that there is a significant volume of product that's being stored at home
with one in three consumers telling us that data security and management is actually stopping
them from recycling. And I don't think that's exclusive to mobile phones. So we're currently
working on a project to expand the product type collected by mobile muster. And our research
indicates that Australians are actually holding on to multiple product streams in their homes.
So at mobile muster, we're taking steps to change consumers' attitudes and behaviors by
developing tools and resources to help educate them on how they can manage that data so that
they can reuse mobiles by selling them or passing them on. Or if they've reached the end of their
useful life, then to recycle them through mobile muster. So from my perspective, I see the role
of product stewardship as an educational one, helping us to tackle the barriers when it comes
to reuse and repair. The data issue isn't going to go away. If anything, with more products being
connected to the internet, there will be increased concern and interest in better managing our data.
So my view is product stewardship should complement the healthy commercial market.
What we know is that regardless of reuse, repair or recycling, consumers want to know that there
are measures in place to ensure their data remains secure and private. So setting repair targets for
schemes like the NTCRS could simply amplify the data issue, increasing products being stored
across the board. And the missed opportunity here is extending the life of these products
through reuse and repair, but also the missed opportunity to recover the resources that go
into making these products. So as we know, for the circular economy to succeed,
we actually need consumers to participate. Thank you, John.
Thank you, Scott. Really good overview of where you're at in your industry with your particular
product class around smartphones and related accessories. If I can just ask one question
of each of you before we go to any other questions from the floor or through Slido, but
trying to focus on, you know, ever focus on solutions and practical measures for consumers.
For each of you, this question, what do you think of the recommendation to explore further the idea
of a consumer facing rating of some sort, not dissimilar to what's happened in France,
but the idea of some sort of star rating along the lines of energy efficiency, star ratings,
water efficiency, the Wells program, major appliances, etc. So from each of you, a quick
response on what you think of that recommendation to look at a star rating for consumers that relates
to repairability, durability, starting with you, Janet.
We're generally supportive, but I guess the one thing that we would ask is please
harmonise with the French regulations and make sure that it's based on international standards
that can be easily compared. I think, you know, a lot of our members already score quite well
on the fix-it ratings that they've got on their website, and so we're generally supportive,
but please not another Australian label. Yes.
Yeah, good point. Ben?
Absolutely agree with Janet. No more labels, right, particularly Australian, purely Australian.
Keep in step with international jurisdictions, nothing special for Australia. Don't get out
of step, particularly with the French arrangements. We've had a lot of experience with the star rating
systems for energy efficiency and water efficiency. They work very well. They're very successful.
Consumers at the point of sale look at those. I think they're number two to price in terms
of selection of products, so it's very successful programs. You could do a lot worse than emulate
some of those elements in those programs. Thanks, Janet.
John, I think, and to Ian's point, and I agree, I think there's examples out there where these
ratings actually do work well and they do benefit consumers, and they're actually quite measurable,
and I think introducing any new labelling or rating shouldn't be subjective. So, from my
perspective, they should actually be measurable and take some learnings from
either what we're seeing in France or the energy rating label system.
Thank you. I've forever got an endless list of questions, but I'm just wondering if there are
any questions from the floor there, Leanne, or through Slido from participants.
Thanks, John. There are some questions that have come through. I'll get Anna to ask some
of the questions, and then we can hand back to you if that's all right. We have been receiving
a number of comments through Slido, and because they're not questions, we're not asking those.
We're not repeating those, if that's okay, just for the audience. I'm sorry.
A genuine question is welcome.
This one's from Kirstie Young. Could there be the notion of recycling drop-off points at the place
of purchase for items which are beyond repair, i.e. JB HiFi, Ted's cameras, et cetera?
Well, yes. I mean, this is already happening, particularly in the battery stewardship space
where the retailers are collecting. The larger items, I'm not sure about large screen TVs and
things, but there is opportunities there. Under the NTCRS, a lot of the retailers are
involved in the scheme, and you can bring your smaller electronics back to the shop
for recycling. For the larger ones, it's problematic from a safety point of view,
and they're usually dropped off at council depots and things.
Retailers are really very active in this space. They're very keen to participate.
Okay. This one's from Connie towards Janet. The IT department in a company wishes to purchase
a product of better stewardship like Canon. However, finance disagrees. How can we solve this?
Oh, gosh. I guess you have to encourage your own sustainability standards, don't you? Really?
This is a complaint that we often have against government, for example. They say you should be
recycling your products, and we say, would you like to buy a refit? Oh, gosh, no. I think you
have to encourage sustainability standards and make sure that they've got meaningful
ratings in your procurement system. That's the only way that I can think to address that.
Thank you. I think that's a really important question. The issue of procurement holds
great potential in terms of improving how procurement takes place, positive procurement,
sustainable procurement, circular procurement. Sometimes it is about making sure, as Janet says,
that there is improved information retraining of procurement professionals in line, often with
organisations' environment sustainability policies. You hear too often that an organisation will have
a position on positive procurement, and somehow it's a major roadblock with the procurement
department, who don't look at the range of factors that need to be assessed in purchasing
products and services. A great question and well answered, Janet. To the procurement department's
defence, they've usually been given a KPI to reduce costs. This question is from Ken.
Many skilled repair techs begin with self-repair. If manufacturers place such onerous barriers on
accessibility, how will they overcome the skill shortage? Sorry, could you just repeat that slowly?
Of course. Many skilled repair techs begin with self-repair. If manufacturers place
such onerous barriers on accessibility, how will they overcome the skill shortage?
Well, I'm in neither industry, but I might just have a go. This is a very issue
that probably Tim spoke about, and we have seen other people speak about the availability
of information and repair manuals. Certainly, this is Carl Wynne's whole business model of providing
information where they reverse engineer products and make that information available.
There is a really strong growing interest in repair, in terms of looking at it through a
STEM industry, like the science, technology, engineering, mathematics skills training that we need
to be able to repair these really highly sophisticated objects. There are those
issues that we recognise, whether they're legal barriers or physical barriers or technological
barriers, but there is certainly a growing willingness among society to become
more trained and more skilled with technologies, I think, as we become more technological as well.
That's certainly not to say that manufacturers are, as we say, taking steps positively to hinder
repair or that education and training that needs to take place. There's lots of really good
examples within, as we say, training schools and skill schools, where there's actually industry
working in partnership with training programs to help develop those skills.
Some of our members have found it increasingly difficult to get skilled people in some of our
sectors, particularly when you get far flung out in the west, something like that. It's almost
to the case where some of our members will not supply products to places like Broken Hill or
Mount Isa, because they know there's no service capability in that area, particularly for products
where you need the person to come to the home, such as washing machines or a fridge or air con.
There's no service capability out in that area. They've made the decision not to supply that area.
I guess if you come at it from another way, the recommendation in the Productivity Commission
report to exempt a manufacturer from liability if a repairer has done something to damage the
product, I think that's an important one, but on the other hand, it's also something that's
really hard to prove often. It's a bit of a can of worms.
I think in tort law, when we talk about it, we talk about a break in the chain of causation.
That's very much looking back at what's the causation of the loss and where is the damage
caused? If there's a break in the chain of causation, then the original party won't be
liable. I think there are legal principles in place to recognise where the manufacturer won't
be liable anymore if there has been a significant repair done. I think that's that whole issue of
is there quality skill in the repair service? I think that's a recognised legal principle.
Mm-hmm. Good. Do we have any other questions from the floor?
Yes, we do. This one is from Erin. Can Janet and Ian please give details on how their
industry's products are getting more durable? This goes against what I've seen and experienced.
Well, washing machines, for example, this is data from Europe that they put to the EU when
they're looking at the new directive, that washing machines are now, they were, in terms of failure
over their lifetime, it was about 9% 10 years ago. Now it's 4%. So they're lasting longer,
they're lasting longer. A lot of these products are lasting longer, far longer than
when it comes to the consumer's preference to replace a product for just getting the
latest technology or for fashion reasons. They just are more durable.
Yes, I haven't got actual sort of hard evidence that I can say, but I know within
Canon certainly the amount of work that goes through our camera workshop has decreased a lot
because the products are very reliable. It's the same for
the multifunction devices or photocopiers that we sell. We
